decision: Use an atomic local JSON snapshot store guarded by an atomic mkdir lock, with per-claim fenced leases using a monotonic mission epoch plus an unguessable UUID token

evaluatedApproaches.name: epoch-plus-uuid-fenced-lease
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: high for the current local durable coordinator; each claim increments a persistent mission-local epoch and receives a unique token, and heartbeat/complete/fail require the current worker plus the current token
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: strong against stale-owner writes after lease expiry/reclaim and after coordinator restart; expired leases are rejected even before explicit requeue
evaluatedApproaches.latency: negligible token-generation and comparison overhead relative to serialized JSON store mutations
evaluatedApproaches.resourceUse: very low; one integer and one token per mission plus UUID generation per claim
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: medium because worker mutation calls now require the lease token; existing durable-queue callers must propagate the token returned by claim
evaluatedApproaches.qa: 8 focused tests pass locally, including restart persistence, concurrent atomic claim, lease recovery, stale-owner rejection, expired-owner rejection, fenced heartbeat, dependency gating, and 8-worker/20-mission contention

evaluatedApproaches.name: uuid-only-lease-token
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: prevents stale claims from matching the current claim when tokens are propagated correctly
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: good, but provides no monotonic generation marker for diagnostics or downstream fencing policies
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: medium because callers still need token propagation
evaluatedApproaches.qa: not selected; weaker observability and future fencing semantics for no meaningful operational savings

evaluatedApproaches.name: worker-id-only-ownership
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: insufficient because a delayed worker identity can remain stale across lease generations and cannot prove possession of the current claim
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: weak under pauses, network partitions, process suspension, and reclaim races
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: low implementation change but high correctness risk
evaluatedApproaches.qa: rejected because stale-owner scenarios are not safely fenced

evaluatedApproaches.name: external-coordinator-issued-global-fencing-sequence
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: strongest future option for truly distributed workers and downstream resource fencing
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: strong if the coordinator is transactional and highly available
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: high for the current lab because worker transport, authentication, and external coordinator semantics are not finalized
evaluatedApproaches.qa: deferred until separate Qubes workers use an authenticated coordinator transport

whyItWon: It directly closes the stale-owner completion/heartbeat gap with minimal runtime cost while retaining a persistent monotonic lease generation for diagnostics and future downstream fencing. It gives stronger correctness and robustness than worker-id or UUID-only ownership without prematurely adding a network coordinator dependency.
knownFailuresAndLessons: The store remains LAB-grade and is not a real multi-host distributed database; workers must share the same filesystem for the lock to coordinate them.
The fenced lease protects mission-state mutations, but it cannot fence side effects performed against an external resource unless that resource also checks the fencing epoch/token.
Whole-state JSON rewrites remain O(n) and will become a throughput bottleneck as mission volume grows.
Stale-lock recovery is time-based and cannot by itself prove that a remote worker is dead.
The selected API intentionally requires claim-token propagation for heartbeat, complete, and fail; any durable-worker adapter must be updated before activation.

Before REAL-WORKER READY, add authenticated worker identities, a Qubes-suitable coordinator/transport, multi-process crash/fault injection with metrics, and downstream side-effect fencing or idempotency controls.
